text:
DeepCrime separates prediction changes from label-grounded failures: a contributing input is correctly predicted by the original model and incorrectly predicted by the mutant. Aggregate killing requires statistical significance plus a minimum effect size across repeated training instances. Configurations not killed by training data are treated as *likely equivalent*, excluded from its mutation-score denominator; this is an empirical screen, not proof of equivalence or unreachability. Trivial and subsumed mutants can inflate scores without adding meaningful testing power. [DeepCrime](https://huang.isis.vanderbilt.edu/cs8395/readings/testing-dl.pdf)

MuFF addresses randomness in both training and mutation application. It checks stability of performance estimates and searches mutation strength to produce killable, challenging mutants; weight/neuron inhibitors permit gradual perturbations. Its reported “sensitivity” measures the difference between strong- and weak-suite mutation scores—not an independent detector’s sensitivity or false-positive rate. Observable behavioral change, statistically established degradation, and detection by a separate oracle therefore require distinct measurements. [MuFF](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.09846v1)

Methodological implication: verify mutation activation and observable effects separately from detector alarms; report inactive, invalid, likely-equivalent and unresolved mutants explicitly. Evaluate a frozen detector against independently established outcomes, including unchanged-model controls for false alarms. Neither mutation score nor output disagreement alone establishes detector accuracy. For correlated inputs, split and quantify uncertainty at the independent unit—such as user, source example or scenario—rather than treating related perturbations as independent evidence. These are evaluation recommendations inferred from the papers’ distinctions, not independently validated detector guarantees from either tool.
